titles: Ancient Sparta Elected Leaders by Shouting
seo.description_hook: How did ancient people vote before ballot boxes? Athenians voted with broken pottery, Spartans shouted, Romans let the rich vote first, and one election ended with the roof torn off a palace.
paragraphs: From ostracism in ancient Athens to the secret ballot in Rome, this is the strange history of voting. We look at the first rigged election, the lottery machine called the kleroterion, and why Athenians thought elections favored the rich.

Then we travel to Sparta's shouting elections, Pompeii's election graffiti, Buddhist voting sticks, the Chola-era kudavolai pot system in Uttaramerur, the Viking Althing, the three-year papal election of Viterbo, and how Venice gave us the word ballot.
Finally, how the secret Australian ballot spread around the world, and when New Zealand became the first country where women voted in national elections.
sources: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians & Politics
Lang, M. - Ostraka, The Athenian Agora vol. 25 (1990)
Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I (c. 919-921 AD)
Mowbray & Gollmann - Electing the Doge of Venice (2007)

scenes.chapter: The Man Who Voted Himself Out

shots.say: Athens, 482 BC. A farmer walks into the city holding a broken piece of pottery.
He can't read. He can't write. But today, he has to vote.
So he walks up to a random stranger and says, excuse me, could you write a name on this for me?
The stranger says, sure. Which name?
And the farmer says, Aristides.
The stranger pauses. Because the stranger... is Aristides.
shots.label: ARISTIDES

shots.say: So he asks, did this Aristides ever do something to you?
And the farmer says, no. I don't even know the guy.
I'm just tired of everyone calling him Aristides the Just.
And Aristides, without saying a word, writes his own name on the pottery and hands it back.
A few days later, Athens kicks him out of the city. For ten years.
And that's one of the oldest voting stories we have. Ancient Greek writer Plutarch tells it.
This week, millions of Americans stood in line to vote.
Paper ballots. Little booths. Stickers that say I voted.
But somebody had to invent all of this. Voting didn't just fall from the sky.

shots.title: HOW PEOPLE VOTED
shots.say: And for most of history, it looked nothing like today.

shots.title: THEY VOTED WITH
shots.say: People voted with broken pots, shouting contests, colored balls, and even swords.
Some elections were rigged. One lasted almost three years. And one ended with people tearing the roof off a palace.
So, how did ancient people actually vote?
Let's start with the place everyone says invented it.

shots.label: ATHENS
shots.say: Ancient Athens, around 500 BC.
The Athenians had a very specific fear. That one guy gets too popular, too rich, and then just takes over.
So they came up with a solution that is honestly kind of genius. And kind of terrifying.

shots.title: THE OSTRACISM VOTE
shots.say: Once a year, they could hold a vote to kick someone out of the city.
No trial. No crime needed. You just write the name of the person you want gone.
And because paper was expensive, they wrote it on broken pottery. Little shards called ostraka.
shots.label: OSTRAKON

shots.say: That's literally where the word ostracize comes from.
The votes were counted, and if there were at least 6,000 shards in total,
whoever had the most votes had ten days to pack and leave. For ten years.
Weirdly, you didn't lose your house or your money. You just had to go away.
Basically, a ten year time out. For adults.
Now, here's where it gets interesting. In 1937, archaeologists were digging near the Acropolis in Athens.
And in an old well, they found about 190 of these shards.
Every single one had the same name on it. Themistocles. A famous Athenian general.
shots.label: THEMISTOCLES

shots.say: Fine. Lots of people didn't like him. That's not weird.
But when experts studied the handwriting, the 190 shards were written by only about 14 people.
So it looks like someone made a big pile of ready made votes, to hand out to people on voting day.
Pre filled ballots. Two and a half thousand years ago.
And the funny part? Those shards were never used. They were just dumped in the well.
But Themistocles did get ostracized later anyway. So I guess it worked eventually.
Okay, but ostracism was the rare, dramatic one. Most of the time, Athenians voted with their hands.
Citizens met on a hill called the Pnyx, sometimes thousands of men at once.
Someone proposed a law, people argued, and then everyone raised a hand.
And nobody counted them one by one. Officials just looked at the crowd and judged which side had more hands.
Which, if you think about it, is just vibes. Very official vibes.
Here's the problem. A lot of people didn't bother showing up. They had farms. And jobs. And honestly, better things to do.
So according to the comic playwright Aristophanes, slaves would sweep the market with a rope dipped in red paint,
and anyone caught with red paint on their clothes, who wasn't at the meeting, could be punished.
shots.label: CAUGHT

shots.say: Later, Athens tried something that works way better. They just paid people to show up.
And suddenly, the meetings were full. Shocking.
Now here's something that will sound completely backwards to us.
The Athenians did not think elections were very democratic.
Because think about it. Who wins elections? The famous guy. The rich guy. The guy who gives the best speeches.
The philosopher Aristotle wrote that choosing by election is how rich people stay in charge.
shots.label: ARISTOTLE

shots.say: Choosing by lottery, on the other hand? That's real democracy.
So for most government jobs, Athens didn't vote at all. They picked random people.
And they built a machine for it. A big stone slab called a kleroterion.
shots.label: KLEROTERION

shots.title: THE LOTTERY MACHINE
shots.say: Citizens put name tokens into slots. Black and white balls dropped down a tube. And the balls decided which rows got picked.
Jury duty. Running the city council. Checking the markets. All random.
Imagine getting a letter saying, congratulations, you are now running the city for a year. Good luck.
But before we call Athens perfect, there's a big catch.

shots.title: WHO COULD VOTE
shots.say: To vote, you had to be a man, over 18, born to Athenian parents, and free.
No women. No slaves. No foreigners, even if they'd lived there their whole lives.
So out of everyone living in Athens, only a small slice could actually vote. Historians usually guess around 10 to 20 percent.
So, democracy. But a very exclusive club version of it.
And the end of ostracism is my favorite story in this whole video.
Around 416 BC, there was a politician named Hyperbolus. And he had a plan.
shots.label: HYPERBOLUS

shots.say: Two powerful men, Nicias and Alcibiades, hated each other. So Hyperbolus called an ostracism vote, hoping one of them would get kicked out.
Then he'd have more power. Simple.
But Nicias and Alcibiades talked to each other. And they made a deal.
They told all their supporters to write the same name. Hyperbolus.
shots.label: HYPERBOLUS

shots.say: So the guy who started the vote got kicked out by his own vote.
And Athens was so embarrassed that, as far as we know, they never used ostracism again.

shots.label: SPARTA
shots.say: Now, while Athens was doing lotteries and pottery, their neighbor Sparta had a very different idea.
Sparta had a council of old men, called the Gerousia. Thirty members, most of them over sixty.
shots.label: GEROUSIA

shots.say: And when a seat opened up, how did they pick the new guy?
They shouted.
The candidates walked through the assembly one at a time, and the crowd yelled for the one they liked.
Meanwhile, a few judges sat locked in a building nearby, where they couldn't see anything.
They just listened, and wrote down which candidate got the loudest shout.
Which means the winner was whoever had the friends with the biggest lungs.
Even Aristotle thought this was childish. And honestly? He's not wrong.

shots.label: ROME
shots.say: A few centuries later, Rome built one of the most complicated voting systems ever.
Romans did vote. Lots. They elected officials every single year.
But there was a twist, and it was very, very Roman.
For the biggest elections, you didn't vote as one person. You voted inside a group, called a century.
shots.label: 1 CENTURY = 1 VOTE

shots.say: Your group decided together, and the whole group counted as one vote.
And there were 193 groups. The rich had lots of small groups. The poor were crammed into a few giant ones.
And the rich groups voted first.
Once a candidate reached a majority, voting just stopped.
So very often, the poorest Romans stood in line all day and never voted at all.
Technically, everyone had a vote. Practically, you could go home.
If you wanted to run for office in Rome, you had to dress the part.
Candidates rubbed their togas with chalk to make them extra white. Bright, clean, trustworthy.
The Latin word for whitened was candidus. And that's where we get the word candidate.
shots.label: CANDIDATUS

shots.say: So every candidate today is basically named after a very clean shirt.
We even have a campaign guide from 64 BC, written for Cicero, probably by his younger brother.
shots.label: 64 BC

shots.title: ROMAN CAMPAIGN TIPS
shots.say: And the advice is a little too familiar.
It basically says, people would rather hear a nice promise than a flat no. So promise.
Two thousand years later, I don't think that book has gone out of date.

shots.label: POMPEII
shots.say: And in Pompeii, we can still read real Roman campaign ads.
When the volcano buried the city in 79 AD, it froze the walls exactly as they were. Covered in painted election slogans.
Thousands of them. Painted on houses, shops, and bars.
Most are boring. Vote for this guy, he's a good man.
But some are amazing. One says, the late night drinkers ask you to elect Marcus Cerrinius Vatia.
Another says, all the deadbeats ask for Vatia.
Historians think these might have been written by his rivals. To make him look bad.
And one is just someone yelling at their friend. Valens, wake up and vote for Sabinus!
Ancient Roman get out the vote. Very aggressive.
For a long time, Roman voting was out loud. You told an official your choice, and everyone heard it.
Which is a problem when your boss, or your landlord, is standing right behind you.

shots.title: SECRET BALLOT
shots.say: So in 139 BC, Rome passed a law for secret voting.
Voters got small wooden tablets covered with wax, and scratched in their choice.
Then they crossed a narrow wooden walkway, a little bridge, and dropped the tablet in a basket.
Cicero called the ballot the silent defender of freedom.
shots.label: CICERO

shots.say: Which is a very fancy way to say, now my landlord can't see what I wrote.

shots.label: INDIA
shots.say: Now let's go to India, where voting showed up in some surprising places.
In early Buddhist monasteries, monks sometimes had to settle disagreements by vote.
And according to Buddhist rules, they used small wooden sticks, called salaka.
shots.label: SALAKA

shots.say: A monk would hand out sticks in different colors, and you voted by picking one.

shots.title: 3 WAYS TO VOTE
shots.say: And the rules even describe three ways to vote.
Secret, whispered in the ear, or completely open. Pretty modern for a monastery.

shots.label: UTTARAMERUR
shots.say: And then there's a village in South India called Uttaramerur.
On the walls of a temple there, there are inscriptions from around 920 AD, under the Chola king Parantaka the First.
And they describe, in great detail, how the village chose its council.

shots.title: THE POT SYSTEM
shots.say: Every candidate's name was written on a palm leaf ticket. The tickets were put in a pot. And a young boy pulled out the winners.

shots.title: RULES TO RUN
shots.say: But not just anyone could put their name in.
And if a council member didn't hand in proper accounts, he was banned. And so were his relatives.
Imagine not being allowed to run because your cousin was bad at math.

shots.label: ICELAND
shots.say: Now, way up north. Iceland, the year 930.
Viking settlers started meeting every summer in an open field, at an assembly called the Althing.
It's often called the oldest parliament in the world that still exists today.
shots.label: ALTHING

shots.say: And when people approved a decision, they didn't raise their hands. They raised their weapons, and clashed them together.
Clang.
There's even an old Norse word for it. Vápnatak. Literally, taking up weapons.
Which is a lot more exciting than an online survey.

shots.label: VITERBO
shots.say: Okay, now the longest election story I know. Italy, 1268.
The Pope had died. And the cardinals met in the town of Viterbo to choose the next one.
There were about 20 of them. And they just could not agree.

shots.title: STILL NO POPE
shots.say: Weeks turned into months. Months turned into years.
So the people of Viterbo got fed up. They locked the cardinals inside the palace.
shots.label: LOCKED

shots.say: Then they cut their food down to bread and water.
And when that still didn't work, they took the roof off the building.
Imagine trying to make a big decision while it's raining on your head.
A few of the cardinals died of old age during the election. Finally, in 1271, they chose a new Pope. Gregory the Tenth.
And Gregory made new rules. From now on, cardinals would be locked in until they chose. With less food the longer they took.
The Latin for with a key is cum clave. Which is why it's still called a conclave today.
shots.label: CONCLAVE
VENICE
shots.say: Meanwhile, Venice had its own way of choosing its leader, the Doge.
And they were so scared of cheating that they made it absurdly complicated.

shots.title: THE DOGE ELECTION
shots.say: From 1268, it went lottery, then vote, then lottery, then vote, again and again, ten rounds, before the final 41 men chose the Doge.
Ten rounds. Just so nobody could buy it.
And for the lottery parts, a young boy was brought in to pull little balls out of a pot, one by one.
In Italian, a little ball was a ballotta.
shots.label: BALLOTTA

shots.say: And that's where the English word ballot comes from.
And in some clubs, you voted with white or black balls in a box. One black ball, and you were out.
Which is where we get the word blackballed.
Now, you'd think once secret voting was invented, everyone kept it. Nope.
For centuries, in lots of places, people voted out loud, in public, in front of everyone.
In England, elections could get rowdy. Candidates bought drinks, and sometimes paid people outright for their votes.
In early America, many people handed in ballots printed by the parties themselves. Often in different colors.
So everyone watching knew exactly how you voted.

shots.label: VICTORIA, 1856
shots.say: The fix came from Australia. In 1856, the colony of Victoria started printing official ballots, filled in privately.
So good, the world called it the Australian ballot.
shots.label: AUSTRALIAN BALLOT

shots.title: SECRET BALLOT ARRIVES
shots.say: Britain adopted it in 1872. American states started in 1888. And Kentucky held on to voting out loud until 1891.
And remember who was missing back in Athens?

shots.label: NEW ZEALAND, 1893
shots.say: In 1893, New Zealand became the first country where women could vote in national elections.
And over the next century, more and more people who were left out, finally got in.
Athens: a small slice of the people. Today: almost every adult.
Two and a half thousand years from pottery shards to paper ballots.
So the next time you stand in a long line to vote, just remember.
At least nobody's chasing you with a rope dipped in red paint.
You don't have to out shout a Spartan.
And nobody's taking the roof off the building.
And please, if someone asks you to write a name on their pottery, check whose name it is first.
Now, if you were in ancient Athens, who would you ostracize? Tell me in the comments.
